entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11491"/><div sID="gen20795" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11491"/><hi type="bold">9-10. open ... from the cities--</hi>I will open up the side, or border of Moab (metaphor from a man whose side is open to blows), from the (direction of) the cities on his northwest border beyond the Arnon, once assigned to Reuben (<reference osisRef="Josh.13.15-Josh.13.21">Jos 13:15-21</reference>), but now in the hands of their original owners; and the "men of the east," the wandering Bedouin hordes, shall enter through these cities into Moab and waste it. Moab accordingly was so wasted by them, that long before the time of Christ it had melted away among the hordes of the desert. For "cities," Grotius translates the Hebrew as proper names, the Ar and Aroer, on the Arnon. Hence the Hebrew for "cities," "Ar" is repeated twice (<reference osisRef="Num.21.28">Nu 21:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.2.36">De 2:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.15.1">Is 15:1</reference>).<div eID="gen20795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20796" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">glory of the country--</hi>The region of Moab was richer than that of Ammon; it answers to the modern Belka, the richest district in South Syria, and the scene in consequence of many a contest among the Bedouins. Hence it is called here a "glorious land" (literally, "a glory," or "ornament of a land") [Fairbairn]. Rather, "the glory of the country" is in apposition with "cities" which immediately precedes, and the names of which presently follow.<div eID="gen20796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20797" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Beth-jeshimoth--</hi>meaning "the city of desolations"; perhaps so named from some siege it sustained; it was towards the west.<div eID="gen20797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20798" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Baal-meon--</hi>called also "Beth-meon" (<reference osisRef="Jer.48.23">Jr 48:23</reference>), and "Beth-baal-meon" (<reference osisRef="Josh.13.17">Jos 13:17</reference>, called so from the worship of Baal), and "Bajith," simply (<reference osisRef="Isa.15.2">Is 15:2</reference>).<div eID="gen20798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20799" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Kiriathaim--</hi>"the double city." The strength of these cities engendered "the pride" of Moab (<reference osisRef="Isa.16.6">Is 16:6</reference>). <div eID="gen20799" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11493"/><div sID="gen20801" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11493"/><hi type="bold">12. taking vengeance--</hi>literally, "revenging with revengement," that is, the most unrelenting vengeance. It was not simple hatred, but deep-brooding, implacable revenge. The grudge of Edom or Esau was originally for Jacob's robbing him of Isaac's blessing (<reference osisRef="Gen.25.23">Ge 25:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.27.27-Gen.27.41">27:27-41</reference>). This purpose of revenge yielded to the extraordinary kindness of Jacob, through the blessing of Him with whom Jacob wrestled in prayer; but it was revived as an hereditary grudge in the posterity of Esau when they saw the younger branch rising to the pre-eminence which they thought of right belonged to themselves. More recently, for David's subjugation of Edom to Israel (<reference osisRef="2Sam.8.14">2Sa 8:14</reference>). They therefore gave vent to their spite by joining the Chaldeans in destroying Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Ps.137.7">Psa 137:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.4.22">La 4:22</reference>; Ob 10-14), and then intercepting and killing the fugitive Jews (<reference osisRef="Amos.1.11">Am 1:11</reference>) and occupying part of the Jewish land as far as Hebron. <div eID="gen20801" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11495"/><div sID="gen20803" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11495"/><hi type="bold">14. by ... my people Israel--</hi>namely, by Judas Maccabeus. The Idumeans were finally, by compulsory circumcision, incorporated with the Jewish state by John Hyrcanus (see <reference osisRef="Isa.34.5">Is 34:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.63.1">63:1</reference>, &c.; 1 Maccabees 5:3). (<reference osisRef="1Sam.13.1-1Sam.14.52">1Sa 13:1-14:52</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.28.18">2Ch 28:18</reference>). The "old hatred" refers to their continual enmity to the covenant-people. They lay along Judea on the seacoast at the opposite side from Ammon and Moab. They were overthrown by Uzziah (<reference osisRef="2Chr.26.6">2Ch 26:6</reference>), and by Hezekiah (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.8">2Ki 18:8</reference>). Nebuchadnezzar overran the cities on the seacoast on his way to Egypt after besieging Tyre (<reference osisRef="Jer.47.1-Jer.47.7">Jr 47:1-7</reference>). God will take vengeance on those who take the avenging of themselves out of His hands into their own (<reference osisRef="Rom.12.19-Rom.12.21">Ro 12:19-21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.2.13">Jas 2:13</reference>). <div eID="gen20804" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11497"/><div sID="gen20805" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11497"/><hi type="bold">16. cut off the Cherethims--</hi>There is a play on similar sounds in the Hebrew, hichratti cherethim, "I will slay the slayers." The name may have been given to a section of the Philistines from their warlike disposition (<reference osisRef="1Sam.30.14">1Sa 30:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.3">31:3</reference>). They excelled in archery, whence David enrolled a bodyguard from them (<reference osisRef="2Sam.8.18">2Sa 8:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.18">15:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.7">20:7</reference>). They sprang from Caphtor, identified by many with Crete, which was famed for archery, and to which the name Cherethim seems akin.
